name: Engine
what: Turns fuel into rotation by burning small amounts of fuel and air in sealed cylinders.
how: Pistons are pushed down by expanding gas on the power stroke; the crankshaft converts that into rotation. Valves, driven by the camshaft, let air in and exhaust out in time with the pistons.
fails: Low oil or overheating can seize it within minutes. Misfires cause shaking and a flashing check-engine light. A snapped timing belt can wreck valves and pistons.

name: Radiator and cooling fan
what: Removes heat from the engine coolant.
how: Hot coolant flows through thin tubes and fins; air passing through — from driving or the electric fan — carries the heat away. A thermostat controls flow so the engine warms up quickly.
when: Constantly, more so in traffic and on hot days.
fails: Leaks, a failed fan or a stuck thermostat lead to overheating. Never open the cap when hot.

name: 12 V battery and alternator
what: The battery starts the engine and powers electrics when it is off; the alternator charges it while the engine runs.
how: The starter motor draws a big current from the battery to crank the engine. Once running, a belt drives the alternator, which supplies the car and recharges the battery.
when: At every start, and for all electrical loads.
fails: Clicking but no cranking: flat battery or poor connection. Battery light while driving: the alternator or its belt has failed — the car will run until the battery is drained.

name: Clutch
what: Connects and disconnects the engine from the gearbox in a manual car.
how: Springs clamp a friction plate between the flywheel and a pressure plate. Pressing the pedal releases the clamp so you can change gear or stop without stalling.
when: Moving off, changing gear and stopping.
fails: A worn clutch slips: revs rise without matching speed. A high biting point or burning smell are warning signs.

name: Gearbox
what: Changes the ratio between engine speed and wheel speed.
how: Pairs of gears of different sizes multiply torque in low gears and let the engine cruise in high gears. Automatics, AMTs, CVTs and DCTs do this without a clutch pedal.
when: All the time the vehicle is moving under power.
fails: Grinding when shifting, jumping out of gear, or delayed and harsh shifts in an automatic.

name: Driveshaft
what: Carries power from the gearbox to the driven wheels or axle.
how: In rear-wheel-drive cars a long propeller shaft runs to the rear axle; in front-wheel-drive cars short shafts with constant-velocity joints run to each front wheel.
fails: Clicking from the front wheels on full lock (worn CV joint) or vibration under acceleration.

name: Differential
what: Lets the wheels on one axle turn at different speeds while sharing torque.
how: A set of bevel gears allows the outer wheel in a turn to spin faster than the inner one. It also contains the final-drive reduction.
when: In every turn, and continuously as the final gear reduction.
fails: Whining that changes with speed, or clunks when taking up drive.

name: Brakes (disc and caliper)
what: Slow and stop the wheels using friction.
how: Pressing the pedal pushes brake fluid to calipers that squeeze pads against a spinning disc. Rear wheels may use drums with shoes. A vacuum or electric booster multiplies your foot's force.
fails: Squeal: pads worn. Grinding: metal on metal. Soft or sinking pedal: air or a leak — stop. Pulsing pedal under light braking: warped discs.

name: ABS / ESC module
what: Prevents wheel lock under hard braking and corrects skids.
how: Wheel-speed sensors feed a control unit that rapidly releases and reapplies the brakes on any wheel about to lock. ESC adds steering and yaw sensors and brakes individual wheels to stop a slide.
when: In emergency braking and on slippery roads.
fails: An amber ABS or ESC light: the system is off but normal brakes still work. Leave bigger gaps.

name: Suspension
what: Keeps the tyres in contact with the road and absorbs bumps.
how: Springs carry the vehicle's weight; dampers control how fast the springs move, stopping the car from bouncing.
when: Constantly, especially on rough roads and in bends.
fails: Bouncing after bumps, clunks, uneven tyre wear and longer braking distances on rough roads.

name: Steering and power assistance
what: Turns the front wheels in response to the steering wheel.
how: The steering column turns a pinion on a toothed rack, which pushes tie rods to angle the wheels. An electric motor (EPS) or hydraulic pump adds assistance.
fails: Heavy steering with a warning light: assistance lost. Play, knocking or pulling: worn joints or alignment.

name: Airbags and seat-belt pretensioners
what: Cushion occupants and hold them in place in a crash.
how: Crash sensors trigger a charge that inflates the airbags in milliseconds and pulls the belts tight. They work together with the seat belt.
when: Only in a crash severe enough to trigger them.
fails: An airbag light means the system may not work in a crash. Have it inspected by trained technicians.

name: Exhaust and catalytic converter
what: Carries exhaust gases away, cleans them and reduces noise.
how: The catalytic converter turns harmful gases into less harmful ones; diesels add a particulate filter. The silencer cuts noise.
fails: Loud roar: a hole or broken joint. Rotten-egg smell or rattling: a failing catalyst. Exhaust smell in the cabin is dangerous (carbon monoxide).

name: Fuel tank and pump
what: Stores fuel and supplies it to the engine at pressure.
how: An electric pump in the tank sends fuel through a filter to the injectors. A vapour system captures fumes.
fails: Running dry can damage the pump; diesels may need bleeding. Fuel smell can mean a leak — stop and investigate.

name: Tyres
what: The only contact between the vehicle and the road.
how: Rubber compounds and tread patterns grip the road and channel water away. Correct pressure keeps the contact patch the right shape.
fails: Low pressure: overheating and blowouts. Worn tread: hydroplaning in rain. Sidewall bulges: imminent failure.
